summary: This informational document describes Media-independent Pre-Authentication (MPA), a secure mobile-assisted way to speed handovers between domains. A device authenticates and sets up configuration with the next network before it moves. It works over any link layer and with any mobility protocol.

eli5.summary: Before walking into a new building, you get your visitor badge by phone, so you don't wait at the door. MPA does this for devices moving between networks.

questions: how to speed up inter-domain handover
subtitle: A framework for speeding handovers when mobile devices move between different network domains.

tldr.problem: When a mobile device moves from one network domain to another, it must authenticate, get a new IP address, and update its mobility protocol binding—operations that take hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, causing packet loss and jitter that disrupt voice and video calls.
tldr.mechanism: Media-Independent Pre-Authentication (MPA) lets the device perform authentication, get an IP address, and establish a tunnel to the new network while still connected to the old one, then complete the move with minimal delay. MPA works over any link layer and with any mobility protocol.
tldr.outcome: Handover delay can be reduced to the link-layer handover time alone, eliminating most of the delay and packet loss that applications experience. MPA is applicable to inter-domain handovers where simultaneous connection to multiple networks is not available.

today: RFC 6252 is an Informational document from the IRTF's IP Mobility Optimizations Research Group. It has not been obsoleted and describes a framework that has influenced subsequent work on optimized handovers. While MPA itself is not standardized as a single protocol, its concepts have been adopted in various mobility optimization schemes in standards bodies and vendor implementations.

sections.title: The Handover Challenge
sections.content:
As wireless technologies proliferate—cellular, WiFi, and others—mobile devices increasingly move between different types of networks and between different administrative domains. A seamless handover requires keeping packets flowing while the device's network attachment changes. However, handovers are costly: the device must discover the new network, authenticate, obtain a new IP address, configure itself, and update its mobility protocol binding. These operations introduce latency and packet loss.

Existing mobility protocols like Mobile IP and Mobile IPv6 maintain a binding between a device's identifier and its current location (called the care-of address), allowing it to continue receiving packets even after moving. But they do not optimize the handover itself. Traditional mobility optimization mechanisms are tightly coupled to specific mobility protocols and assume pre-established security associations between administrative domains—assumptions that do not hold in many real networks, particularly when domains belong to different operators.

The Media-Independent Pre-Authentication (MPA) framework addresses these limitations. MPA is a mobile-assisted, secure handover optimization scheme that works over any link layer and with any mobility management protocol.
sections.eli5: Moving between networks is slow because the device has to go through several steps: say hello to the new network, prove it is allowed to connect, get an address, and tell everyone where it moved. MPA lets the device do these steps while still on the old network.

sections.title: How MPA Works
sections.content:
MPA operates in several phases. In the pre-authentication phase, the mobile node discovers candidate target networks (networks it might move to) and establishes a security association with an authentication agent in each one. This creates trust without requiring a pre-arranged relationship between the domains.

In the pre-configuration phase, while still attached to the old network, the device obtains an IP address from the candidate target network and establishes a proactive handover tunnel—an IP tunnel back to the new network's access router. This tunnel allows the device to send and receive packets using the new network's IP address while still physically attached to the old network.

In the secure proactive handover phase, the device can complete its mobility protocol binding update and send data traffic over the tunnel using the new IP address, all before physically moving. When the device finally performs the link-layer handover (switches to the new network), it deletes the tunnel and assigns the new IP address directly to its physical interface. Since most of the handover work is done beforehand, only the link-layer handover delay remains.

MPA's key innovation is that it decouples the layer 3 (IP) and layer 4+ (mobility protocol) operations from the layer 2 (link-layer) handover, allowing them to complete proactively.
sections.eli5: Before moving: authenticate with the new network, get an address, and open a tunnel. While moving: complete the mobility protocol updates through the tunnel. After moving: switch to the new network and close the tunnel. Most work happens before the physical move.

sections.title: Discovery and Multi-Target Handovers
sections.content:
A critical part of MPA is discovering which networks the device might move to. Methods include the Candidate Access Router Discovery (CARD) protocol, Service Location Protocol (SLP), link-layer management frames sent by access points, and IEEE 802.21 mobility servers. Once candidate networks are identified, the device can perform discovery and proactive operations in advance.

In practice, a device may not always move to the network it expects. The RFC describes how MPA handles this: the device can pre-authenticate with multiple candidate target networks, obtaining IP addresses and establishing tunnels with several of them. If the device ends up moving to a different candidate network than it predicted, it is already prepared. Alternatively, the device can use simultaneous mobility binding to send multiple binding updates to the home agent, allowing it to receive traffic from multiple networks temporarily until it settles on the final destination.

The document emphasizes that proactive IP address acquisition is critical to reducing handover delay. Methods include PANA-assisted address acquisition, IKEv2-assisted acquisition, and stateless IPv6 autoconfiguration. All allow the device to obtain and configure an address proactively, eliminating this delay from the actual handover.
sections.eli5: The device learns which networks are nearby and picks candidates. It can pre-authenticate with several of them and be ready for any of them. If it guesses wrong and moves somewhere else, it can quickly switch.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Issues
sections.content:
MPA security is based on establishing a shared key between the mobile node and the authentication agent, typically using an authentication protocol carrying EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol). Keys derived from this shared secret protect subsequent configuration and tunnel management messages. Because MPA does not require pre-established relationships between administrative domains, it can work between independent operators.

The RFC identifies several deployment considerations. Failed switching can occur when a device begins handover preparation but the signal to the target network fails before the physical handover completes. MPA must handle switching back to the original network. Authentication state management ensures that pre-authenticated security associations have appropriate lifetimes and are cleaned up if handover does not occur. QoS resource pre-allocation is optional but can improve performance by reserving bandwidth in advance.

The document notes that MPA effectiveness may be reduced in networks that already support optimized mobility, such as those with network-controlled localized mobility management where devices do not change IP addresses within a domain. MPA is most valuable for inter-domain handovers where the device must obtain a new address and each domain may use a different mobility protocol.
sections.eli5: The device and new network prove they trust each other before moving. Different operators do not need to trust each other beforehand. If the device changes its mind and switches back, the system handles it. The system can reserve resources in advance if needed.

sections.title: Performance Goals and Applicability
sections.content:
MPA targets seamless handovers suitable for real-time voice and video. The document specifies performance requirements: for interactive VoIP, ITU-T standard G.114 recommends a maximum one-way delay of 150 ms for most applications and 400 ms as generally unacceptable. Voice can tolerate up to 2% packet loss; video requires lower loss and delay. Handover delay—the combined effect of discovery, authentication, address acquisition, and binding update—contributes directly to these metrics.

MPA is most applicable where accurate movement prediction is feasible: planned handovers on known routes, not random indoor roaming. In environments with predictable mobility patterns, MPA can reduce total handover delay to approximately the link-layer handover time alone, which is typically 50–200 ms depending on the technology.

The RFC also notes that MPA is a framework, not a specific protocol. It specifies what functionality must occur—pre-authentication, pre-configuration, secure proactive handover—but leaves to future work the choice of specific protocols to implement each component. An accompanying document describes one realization using existing protocols.
sections.eli5: Voice calls can only tolerate about 150 milliseconds of delay without problems. MPA tries to keep delays low by preparing everything before the physical switch. It works best when you can predict where devices will move.
